title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows an AI coding and agent tool being used outside the conditions it was built for. Cursor Agent, which runs on Claude Sonnet, was designed to assist with software development tasks. The Aurora ransomware group directed it instead toward offensive security operations: configuring VPNs for intrusion, scanning networks, enumerating domains, and executing NTLM relay attacks against target organizations.

The failure is misuse rather than a malfunction in the conventional sense. The tool performed the tasks it was asked to perform, including tasks that fell outside any legitimate development context. The point where this could have been caught is at the task-acceptance layer, where a system capable of executing network and authentication commands against external infrastructure would need guardrails distinguishing authorized environments from hostile ones. Many commands reportedly failed on first attempts, which indicates the agent was being used iteratively in an adversarial context rather than a controlled one.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic had specific knowledge of this abuse before it was reported, or whether the tool's safeguards were deliberately bypassed versus simply not present for this class of action.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified Aurora ransomware group operations targeting ESXi environments since April 2026. The group deployed a Linux ransomware variant capable of encrypting virtual machine files while keeping hypervisors bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Aurora operators also abused Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct exploitation activities across ten target organizations between April and May 2026. The agent assisted with tasks including VPN configuration, network scanning, domain enumeration, and NTLM relay attacks, though many commands failed on first attempts.

A second Aurora cluster was identified with medium confidence, affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries. This cluster used different tactics including SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation with GodPotato, and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. The article provides technical indicators of compromise including IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes associated with both attack clusters to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware activities.
